title: Polyamory: When two just won't do
summary: Josh and Chuck explain polyamory: consensual, committed relationships among more than two people, distinguished from cheating, swinging, open relationships, and polygamy. They cover evolutionary theories of monogamy in mammals, the benefits of a larger support network, how polyamorous relationships are structured (triads, quads, hierarchical vs. equal "primary/secondary" arrangements, veto power), handling jealousy and communication, compersion, STI testing and fluid-bonded arrangements, research findings on satisfaction and longevity, social stigma and child custody risks, demographics, the Oneida Commune history, and a listener mail segment about pu-erh tea.

segments.title: Opening banter and defining polyamory
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce polyamory and explain it is not cheating, swinging, or polygamy; it is a committed, consensual arrangement among more than two people. They mention monogamish, a term coined by Dan Savage.

segments.title: Evolutionary theories of monogamy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why monogamy is evolutionarily puzzling, noting only about five percent of mammal species are monogamous. They cover three theories: males guarding offspring from infanticide, low female density and paternity certainty, and lesser males using paternal care as a strategy.

segments.title: Benefits of polyamory
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss benefits: more support and emotional care from a larger network, sexual variety, and polyamorous relationships that are not necessarily sexual (polyamorous-affective ties). A story describes a woman whose varied interests were met by multiple partners.

segments.title: Communication, jealousy and logistics
segments.summary: Polyamory requires strong communication and honesty about feelings. The hosts describe deconstructing jealousy, the logistical complexity of scheduling multiple partners, and the plural of spouse being spice. Research by Terri Conley is cited: jealousy is lower among polyamorous and non-monogamous people than monogamous pairs.

segments.title: Open relationships, swinging, and sexual satisfaction
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish open relationships from polyamorous groups, which form a closed unit. They cite research on sexual satisfaction and relationship longevity, and mention swinging's history among World War Two Air Force servicemen and the Atlantis Swingers Club phone number.

segments.title: STI testing, structures, and rules
segments.summary: Polyamorous groups are described as very open about STI testing, more so than new monogamous couples, and as relying on rules. The hosts describe equal groups versus hierarchical structures with primary, secondary, and tertiary partners, veto power, and body-fluid monogamy arrangements.

segments.title: Compersion, stability, and stigma
segments.summary: The hosts define compersion as joy at a partner's happiness with someone else. They discuss how marriage stability differs by reasons given, and social stigma, including a custody case involving a polyamorous family, the lack of research on children raised polyamorously, and demographics such as education levels and the 'hunting the unicorn' phenomenon.

segments.title: Oneida Community history
segments.summary: Josh describes the Oneida Community, a free-love commune founded by John Humphrey Noyes in upstate New York in the 1840s, which encouraged multiple partners and had religious undertones, and notes the Oneida silverware company descended from it.

segments.title: Listener mail: pu-erh tea
segments.summary: A listener points out that the show omitted pu-erh, a fermented tea from Yunnan Province, China, which can be aged for years and is sold in pressed disc form.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and point to website, social media, and email contact options.
